Major Gargett, meanwhile, seemed to have understood nothing. As though somebody had put a spell on him, he swung the neck of that cumbersome giant this way and that. From the movements I could almost see the blank face inside.

His men seemed no better. Not one could answer the commander. Not one could stop copying him.

Then his giant froze, facing one point. The same as mine. Fudaraku Castle, looking much too large.

In half a second, he would have the answer he wanted. His men would take a few seconds more.

For now, then, there was still this last peace.

Not knowing what had come. Not knowing what had happened. Still able to exist without terror, without madness, without breaking.
Precious time.

Time that would not come back.
The last. The very last.

They raged.
Whatever was nearest, they attacked.

One infantryman sprayed machine-gun fire into his own colleagues. A tank came from behind and crushed him.

That tank turned its main gun on another of the same model ahead. Before it could fire, someone threw a grenade down the muzzle. Fire roared out; the tank blew apart.

The one it had aimed at took no notice at all. It kept scattering shells into the sky. Hitting a highly mobile warrior like that was no easy matter. But one shell finally tore through an S-14 Werewolf's wing.

A craft tumbled from the sky. Its companions could only stare.
They had not become beasts.

The warriors inside adamantine armor—only they, in this little world, were discovering how helpless a human being could be without protection.

Major Gargett was among the calmest, still repeating his useless commands. Perhaps that was precisely what made him stand out. To the beasts, perhaps he looked especially worth eating.

Something precious to him, something he believed in, was collapsing. With which words had he intended to hold it up?

Silver.
White silver.
Pure silver steel.

A piece of the moon, people had believed.
A metal with magic in it, they had feared.
A metal that led to madness, they had shunned.

Simple beliefs of ancient people. Modern positivism had come with its savage sword and cut the whole thing dead.

Ignorance. Superstition. Imagination.

Achha. And which side was the ignorant one?

Silver stood here, now.

The moon's beauty.
The sorcerer's strength.
The light of madness.

Nothing missing.
The silver warrior was here.

After this, how to doubt?
How to throw away that faith in silver?

She said it, and vanished from the middle of the encirclement.
Not even a trail of smoke left behind.

No sorcery.
She had flown out. That was all.

Only, her acceleration and turning were so far beyond the ordinary that an ordinary eye could register nothing but disappearance. The occupation warriors were staring in confusion and shock.

Only the Silver Star, with her control of gravity, could move like that.
And now she was coming.

I braced myself.
What resistance this amounted to, I knew very well.

The next time I saw silver, I might already be in two pieces. There would be no use complaining that this was unreasonable.

But it did not happen.

She appeared at the storm's center.
On top of the monster.

Sitting there with perfect grace, she raised a hand.
Between her fingers, light appeared.
